newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Thousands of rifles, pistols at large in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of rifles, pistols at large in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO soldiers keeping the lid on Bosnia's warring factions believe they have tracked down all tanks and heavy artillery, but thousands of rifles and pistols are missing and presumed ready for action.
Police who once had anti-tank missiles in their stations are now down to one pistol each. The big guns are being confined to storage sites and regularly checklisted by NATO troops.

"They are very, very compliant," said Captain Norrie Robertson, a British intellilgence officer working out of a makeshift barracks in the bus depot in Mrkonjic Grad, about 130 km (80 miles) northeast of Sarajevo.
"We are convinced we have the lid on heavy weapons. There are no tanks and artillery out there but there could be thousands of rifles and pistols," he said.
"We know there are weapons in the villages but our mandate is not to kick down their doors and go looking for them. We can do nothing unless we see someone with a rifle."

Dramatic proof was provided over Christmas and the New Year when scores of rifles rounds were fired around town in what the military called "celebratory fire". Barracks were criss-crossed with gunfire.
Soldiers with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's 31,000-strong Stabilisation Force (SFOR) say the hatred is still palpable in the areas where the 43-month war was so bitterly fought out.
"If SFOR was not here, there would be problems," Robertson said of the NATO troops who have an 18-month mandate to help reconstruct Bosnia after a war that left tens of thousands dead.

"The Serbs are paranoid about an attack from the Moslem-Croat federation. We are keeping the lid on it by being here," Robertson said on a visit to the snow-shrouded garrison by British Defence Minister Michael Portillo.

At British headquarters in nearby Serb-held Banja Luka, the Royal Military Police put on display an array of seized weapons ranging pistols to rocket-launchers. They have confiscated 75 weapons in the last six months.
"The thing that is really surprising is the weapons we have confiscated from police stations," Lieutenant-Colonel John Baber said.
"A police Land Rover we stopped was armed with twin 20mm anti-aircraft guns. Police officers were not surprised at having anti-tank mines in their stations and crates of grenades."
The U.S.-led "train and equip" military aid programme for the Moslem-Croat federation causes consternation and anger among the Serbs.
Baber is the first to admit it also poses problems for him.
"It is something very difficult to explain to the people we are dealing with. The average man on the street finds it difficult to understand the dichotomy," he said.
What, then, are the chances of peace holding once NATO has left?
"The people will tell you it is a tentative peace," Baber said.
"They know we are here on a finite mission. They all say to you that in 18 months it will start all over again. If we get it wrong -- as far as they are concerned -- it will be solved militarily."
